title: Sleeping Bear Dunes
subtitle: THE MOST BEAUTIFUL PLACE IN AMERICA YOU'VE NEVER HEARD OF

scenes.text: In twenty eleven, Good Morning America asked viewers to vote for the most beautiful place in America. They didn't pick the Grand Canyon. They didn't pick Yosemite. They picked this.
Sleeping Bear Dunes, on the northwest coast of Michigan. Water this blue, sand this white, and most people have never even heard of it.
The park runs along sixty-five miles of shoreline, counting the two wild islands sitting out in the lake.
And yes, that is a lake. Lake Michigan is so big you can't see the other side, and on a calm summer day its water turns a shade of turquoise you'd expect in the Caribbean.
The name comes from an Anishinaabe legend. A mother bear and her two cubs swam across the lake to escape a forest fire on the far shore.

The mother reached land and lay down on the bluff to wait. Her cubs never made it. Two islands rose where they sank, North and South Manitou, and the wind buried the mother beneath the sand. She is the sleeping bear.
The landscape itself was shaped by ice. At the end of the last ice age, retreating glaciers left behind enormous piles of sand and rock along this coast.
Over thousands of years, the wind pushed sand up onto the bluffs, building what geologists call perched dunes, sitting high above the water.
The tallest rise about four hundred and fifty feet. From the top, the drop to the water looks like the edge of the world.
It is also a trap. Every summer, visitors run down the dune to the beach, then realise the only way out is straight back up, through loose sand, in the heat.
Some can't make it. The local fire department charges for rescues, and the bill can reach two thousand seven hundred dollars.
Out in the lake sit the Manitou Islands. South Manitou has a lighthouse built in eighteen seventy-one, which guided ships through the Manitou Passage. Dozens of shipwrecks still lie in these waters.
North Manitou is almost entirely wilderness. No cars, no roads for visitors, just forest and empty beach.
Behind the dunes the land turns to deep forest. The park holds twenty-six inland lakes and more than nine hundred kinds of plants.
In October, those forests explode into color, red, orange and gold, right down to the shore.
Hidden among the trees are the farms of Port Oneida. The families who settled here in the eighteen hundreds are long gone, but many of their barns and farmhouses still stand.
Then winter arrives, and everything changes. Snow settles on the dunes, the lake turns steel blue, and the beaches empty out.
But any time of year, the best show is at sunset, when the sun sinks straight into Lake Michigan and the dunes glow pink.
About one and a half million people visit each year. That sounds like a lot, until you see how much space there is. It still feels like a secret.
Sleeping Bear Dunes became a National Lakeshore in nineteen seventy, protected so it can look like this for generations.
So, would you climb back up that dune, or call for the rescue? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for more of America's hidden places.

In 2011, Good Morning America viewers voted Sleeping Bear Dunes the most beautiful place in America. Most people still have never heard of it.

Fly over 450-foot sand dunes, turquoise Lake Michigan water, the wild Manitou Islands, October forests and winter dunes, and hear the Anishinaabe legend behind the name.
